claim: The ER membrane protein complex (EMC) was first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as an abundant and stable multi-protein membrane complex.
source: It was first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as an abundant and stable multi-protein membrane complex whose disruption results in stress mirroring that caused by misfolded membrane proteins (Jonikas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jonikas et al., 2009.

claim: Disruption of the EMC in Saccharomyces cerevisiae results in stress mirroring that caused by misfolded membrane proteins.
source: It was first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as an abundant and stable multi-protein membrane complex whose disruption results in stress mirroring that caused by misfolded membrane proteins (Jonikas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jonikas et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of the EMC in mammalian cells is associated with failed biogenesis and degradation of a subset of membrane proteins.
source: Loss of the EMC in mammalian cells is associated with failed biogenesis and degradation of a subset of membrane proteins (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Christianson et al., 2012.

claim: The EMC has been implicated in several mechanistically distinct steps of membrane protein biogenesis, stabilization, and quality control.
source: Accordingly, the EMC has been implicated in several mechanistically distinct steps of membrane protein biogenesis, stabilization, and quality control (Bircham et al., 2011; Richard et al., 2013; Satoh et al., 2015; Savidis et al., 2016; Shurtleff et al., 2018; Volkmar et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: EMC's insertase function has been demonstrated for low hydrophobicity tail-anchored proteins.
source: EMC's insertase function has been demonstrated for two classes of clients: low hydrophobicity tail-anchored proteins (i.e. those that contain C-terminal membrane anchors) and a subset of polytopic transmembrane proteins in which the first helix is inserted with the N-terminus in the lumen (Guna et al., 2018; Chitwood et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guna et al., 2018 and Chitwood et al., 2018.

claim: EMC's insertase function has been demonstrated for a subset of polytopic transmembrane proteins in which the first helix is inserted with the N-terminus in the lumen.
source: EMC's insertase function has been demonstrated for two classes of clients: low hydrophobicity tail-anchored proteins (i.e. those that contain C-terminal membrane anchors) and a subset of polytopic transmembrane proteins in which the first helix is inserted with the N-terminus in the lumen (Guna et al., 2018; Chitwood et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guna et al., 2018 and Chitwood et al., 2018.

claim: The EMC has been implicated in the biogenesis and stability of many membrane protein classes that do not require a terminal transmembrane insertase.
source: The EMC has been implicated in the biogenesis and stability of many membrane protein classes that do not require a terminal transmembrane insertase (Bircham et al., 2011; Louie et al., 2012; Richard et al., 2013; Shurtleff et al., 2018; Coelho et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2002; Volkmar et al., 2019; Talbot et al., 2019; Petkovic et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The EMC is required for stability of internal transmembrane helices of human and viral multi-pass membrane proteins.
source: Recent studies have shown that the EMC is required for stability of internal transmembrane helices of human and viral multi-pass membrane proteins (Hiramatsu et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2019; Ngo et al., 2019; Coelho et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The human EMC physically interacts with the NS4A-B region of the Dengue Virus polyprotein following Sec61-dependent translocation and signal peptidase cleavage.
source: Additionally, the human EMC (hEMC) physically interacts with the NS4A-B region of the Dengue Virus polyprotein following Sec61-dependent translocation and signal peptidase cleavage, suggesting roles in post-translational stabilization of polytopic membrane proteins (Ngo et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ngo et al., 2019 and Lin et al., 2019.

claim: The S. cerevisiae EMC co-immunoprecipitated with full-length polytopic transmembrane clients, including Pma1p, Mrh1p, and Fks1p.
source: Similarly, the S. cerevisiae EMC (yEMC) co-immunoprecipitated with full-length polytopic transmembrane clients, including Pma1p (Luo et al., 2002), Mrh1p, and Fks1p (Shurtleff et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2002 and Shurtleff et al., 2018.

claim: The EMC associates with a range of regulatory factors, including many general and substrate-specific chaperones in the cytoplasm and in the ER lumen.
source: In addition to varying types of transmembrane protein clients, the EMC also associates with a range of regulatory factors, including many general and substrate-specific chaperones in the cytoplasm and in the ER lumen (Bagchi et al., 2016; Coelho et al., 2019; Kudze et al., 2018; Richard et al., 2013; Shurtleff et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The EMC is an eight (yeast) or nine (mammalian) component, 248–284 kDa complex with considerable mass in the ER lumen, membrane, and cytosol.
source: The EMC is an eight (yeast) or nine (mammalian) component, 248–284 kDa complex with considerable mass in the ER lumen, membrane, and cytosol.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of the EMC contains conserved tetratricopeptide repeats (TPR) repeats in EMC2.
source: The cytoplasmic domain contains conserved tetratricopeptide repeats (TPR) repeats in EMC2, and the human complex accommodates an additional subunit, EMC8/9, whose function is not yet understood.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The human EMC complex accommodates an additional subunit, EMC8/9, whose function is not yet understood.
source: The cytoplasmic domain contains conserved tetratricopeptide repeats (TPR) repeats in EMC2, and the human complex accommodates an additional subunit, EMC8/9, whose function is not yet understood.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The ER lumenal domain in yeast does not contain an N-terminal EMC1 expansion seen in hEMC.
source: The ER lumenal domain in yeast does not contain an N-terminal EMC1 expansion seen in hEMC.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The ER lumenal domain has been linked to a number of disease-associated phenotypes.
source: Notably, the ER lumenal domain has been linked to a number of disease-associated phenotypes (Junes-Gill et al., 2011; Probert et al., 2015; Harel et al., 2016; Abu-Safieh et al., 2013; Diamantopoulou et al., 2017; Marquez et al., 2020), and presents the possibility of additional functions for the human lumenal domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: EMC3 shares limited sequence homology with a family of insertases that are evolutionarily related to the bacterial insertase YidC.
source: One EMC subunit (EMC3) shares limited sequence homology with a family of insertases that are evolutionarily related to the bacterial insertase YidC (Samuelson et al., 2000; Kumazaki et al., 2014; Borowska et al., 2015; Anghel et al., 2017), perhaps explaining the insertase function of the complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: High-resolution cryo-EM structures of yeast EMC bound to a Fab were determined.
source: Here, we determined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of yeast EMC bound to a Fab and two conformations of the human EMC structure.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Two conformations of the human EMC structure were determined.
source: Here, we determined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of yeast EMC bound to a Fab and two conformations of the human EMC structure.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Both yEMC and hEMC structures reveal a path for transmembrane helix insertion from the cytoplasm into the membrane via a conserved cavity.
source: Both yEMC and hEMC structures reveal a path for transmembrane helix insertion from the cytoplasm into the membrane via a conserved cavity.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The EMC structures revealed a second lipid-filled cavity with regions of importance for all three client types probed.
source: Our structures and mutants also revealed a second lipid-filled cavity with regions of importance for all three client types probed.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural and mutational data presented.

claim: Analysis of human disease mutations in hEMC1 and structure-informed mutations enabled decoupling of the EMC insertase function from non-insertase functions.
source: Analysis of human disease mutations in hEMC1 and our structure-informed mutations enabled us to decouple the EMC insertase function from non-insertase functions and reveal a potential role of the EMC in differentially controlling the biogenesis of distinct classes of client proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: The EMC has a potential role in differentially controlling the biogenesis of distinct classes of client proteins.
source: Analysis of human disease mutations in hEMC1 and our structure-informed mutations enabled us to decouple the EMC insertase function from non-insertase functions and reveal a potential role of the EMC in differentially controlling the biogenesis of distinct classes of client proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: The EMC adopts a modular architecture enabling its diverse functions in membrane protein biogenesis.
source: These structure-function studies collectively establish that the EMC adopts a modular architecture enabling its diverse functions in membrane protein biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural and functional data presented.

claim: FLAG affinity-tagging of the EMC5 C-terminus was performed for endogenous yEMC and recombinant hEMC in human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells.
source: Parallel efforts converged on an approach involving FLAG affinity-tagging of the EMC5 C-terminus, which was performed for endogenous yEMC and recombinant hEMC in human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the methods described.

claim: The yEMC and hEMC structures are comprised of cytoplasmic, transmembrane, and lumenal domains arranged similarly for yeast and human.
source: The EMC is comprised of cytoplasmic, transmembrane, and lumenal domains arranged similarly for yeast and human, despite significant evolutionary separation (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: For both yeast and human EMC, subunits encompassing EMC2 to EMC7 form an interconnected core complex.
source: For both species, subunits encompassing EMC2 to EMC7 form an interconnected core complex, while there is additional density capping both the cytoplasmic and lumenal domains of hEMC, occupied by an hEMC8/9 and an hEMC1 N-terminal expansion, respectively (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: There is additional density capping both the cytoplasmic and lumenal domains of hEMC, occupied by an hEMC8/9 and an hEMC1 N-terminal expansion, respectively.
source: For both species, subunits encompassing EMC2 to EMC7 form an interconnected core complex, while there is additional density capping both the cytoplasmic and lumenal domains of hEMC, occupied by an hEMC8/9 and an hEMC1 N-terminal expansion, respectively (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: hEMC8 and hEMC9 are paralogs of each other, which have not been identified in yeast.
source: hEMC8 and hEMC9 are paralogs of each other, which have not been identified in yeast (Wideman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wideman, 2015.

claim: The large hEMC1 insertion in hEMC constitutes the majority of a membrane distal beta-propeller domain protruding into the lumen, a feature missing from S. cerevisiae.
source: The large hEMC1 insertion in hEMC constitutes the majority of a membrane distal beta-propeller domain protruding into the lumen, a feature missing from S. cerevisiae.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The arrangement of domains of the EMC is unusual with the transmembrane domain connecting prominent cytoplasmic and lumenal domains.
source: Compared to other ER-resident proteins implicated in membrane protein biogenesis (Suloway et al., 2009; Pfeffer et al., 2017; Ramírez et al., 2019; McDowell et al., 2020; McGilvray et al., 2020), the arrangement of domains of the EMC is unusual with the transmembrane domain connecting prominent cytoplasmic and lumenal domains (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by comparison to other structures.

claim: The exterior interface of the cytoplasmic domain is formed by EMC2, EMC3, EMC4, and parts of hEMC8/9 (in human).
source: The exterior interface of the cytoplasmic domain is formed by EMC2, EMC3, EMC4, and parts of hEMC8/9 (in human), while parts of EMC5, EMC2, and EMC8/9 are shielded from the cytoplasm (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Parts of EMC5, EMC2, and EMC8/9 are shielded from the cytoplasm.
source: The exterior interface of the cytoplasmic domain is formed by EMC2, EMC3, EMC4, and parts of hEMC8/9 (in human), while parts of EMC5, EMC2, and EMC8/9 are shielded from the cytoplasm (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The helical fold of EMC2 constitutes the central organizer of the cytoplasmic platform, established by five or six TPR motifs in human versus yeast, respectively.
source: The helical fold of EMC2 constitutes the central organizer of this platform, established by five or six TPR motifs in human versus yeast, respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: TPR domains are commonly found mediating protein-protein interactions and are present in numerous well-characterized chaperone-protein and other interaction networks.
source: TPR domains are commonly found mediating protein-protein interactions and are present in numerous well-characterized chaperone-protein and other interaction networks (Blatch and Lässle, 1999; Scheufler et al., 2000; Schlegel et al., 2007; Assimon et al., 2015; Krysztofinska et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Yeast EMC2 features a more curved helical arrangement with N- and C-terminal domains in closer proximity to each other than seen in hEMC2.
source: Yeast EMC2 features a more curved helical arrangement with N- and C-terminal domains in closer proximity to each other than seen in hEMC2.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The canonical peptide-binding TPR groove is occupied by the partially helical C-terminus of EMC5.
source: Notably, the canonical peptide-binding TPR groove is occupied by the partially helical C-terminus of EMC5, which forms a large interaction surface with EMC2.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The C-terminus of EMC5 forms a large interaction surface with EMC2.
source: Notably, the canonical peptide-binding TPR groove is occupied by the partially helical C-terminus of EMC5, which forms a large interaction surface with EMC2.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The hEMC2K125E + R126D + K127E mutation decreased hEMC integrity by western blot, with a strong reduction in the levels of several hEMC subunits.
source: The mutations on both sides of the interface decreased hEMC integrity by western blot, with a modest decrease of hEMC subunits for hEMC5F90A and a strong reduction in the levels of several hEMC subunits for hEMC2K125E + R126D + K127E (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplements 5–6).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the western blot data presented.

claim: The hEMC5F90A mutation decreased hEMC integrity by western blot, with a modest decrease of hEMC subunits.
source: The mutations on both sides of the interface decreased hEMC integrity by western blot, with a modest decrease of hEMC subunits for hEMC5F90A and a strong reduction in the levels of several hEMC subunits for hEMC2K125E + R126D + K127E (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplements 5–6).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the western blot data presented.

claim: The EMC2-EMC5 interface might be critical for EMC complex assembly rather than EMC function.
source: This suggests that this interface might be critical for EMC complex assembly rather than EMC function.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is an inference based on the mutational data.

claim: The EMC presents two distinct and structurally conserved cavities on opposite sides of the transmembrane core that differ in size, shape, subunit compositions and apparent function.
source: The EMC presents two distinct and structurally conserved cavities on opposite sides of the transmembrane core that differ in size, shape, subunit compositions and apparent function (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: One cavity, referred to as the lipid-filled cavity, appears contiguous with the ER lipid environment.
source: One cavity, which we refer to as the lipid-filled cavity, appears contiguous with the ER lipid environment (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The second cavity, referred to as the gated cavity, appears to open toward the cytoplasm in the EMC structures and is more occluded by a transmembrane helix gate from the lipid environment.
source: The second cavity, which we refer to as the gated cavity, appears to open toward the cytoplasm in our structures and is more occluded by a transmembrane helix gate from the lipid environment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Notable structural hallmarks present in both yeast and human EMC include a superimposable core of nine transmembrane helices, a set of flexible gate helices, and an amphipathic EMC1 brace helix.
source: Notable structural hallmarks present in both species include a superimposable core of nine transmembrane helices, a set of flexible gate helices, and an amphipathic EMC1 brace helix (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The gated cavity has a cavernous opening at the membrane-cytoplasmic interface, wide enough to allow passage of a client helix, and tapering toward the lumen.
source: Evaluating potential client paths from the cytoplasm into the transmembrane domain revealed a cavernous opening at the membrane-cytoplasmic interface of the gated cavity, wide enough to allow passage of a client helix, and tapering toward the lumen (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The EMC3 portion of the cytoplasmic domain sits approximately 45 Å from the lumenal side of the gated cavity.
source: Consistent with its potential role as a cytoplasmic conduit into the EMC, the EMC3 portion of the cytoplasmic domain, which delineates this opening, sits approximately 45 Å from the lumenal side of the gated cavity.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The dimension of the gated cavity exceeds the thickness of the ER membrane.
source: This dimension exceeds the thickness of the ER membrane (Mitra et al., 2004; Heberle et al., 2020; Cornell et al., 2020; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data and citations.

claim: The gated cavity is lined primarily by EMC3, EMC4, and EMC6.
source: This cavity is lined primarily by EMC3, EMC4, and EMC6 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: There is sufficient space in the gated cavity for a client helix even in the client-free state of the EMC.
source: Simulating the dimension of the first transmembrane helix of a known terminal insertase-client (B1AR - Chitwood et al., 2018) suggests that there is sufficient space for a client helix even in the client-free state of the EMC (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data and modeling.

claim: The gated cavity is hydrophilic on the cytoplasmic side and becomes increasingly hydrophobic toward the lumenal side.
source: The gated cavity is hydrophilic on the cytoplasmic side and becomes increasingly hydrophobic toward the lumenal side (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Charge swap mutations along the rim of the gated cavity entrance (hEMC3E63K + D213K + E223K, hEMC3R59E + R62E + K216E) resulted in loss of the tail-anchored client (SQS378-410) and partial loss of the N-terminal insertase-dependent polytopic client (B1AR).
source: To test its function, charge swap mutations were introduced along the rim of this opening (hEMC3E63K + D213K + E223K, hEMC3R59E + R62E + K216E) (Figure 5D). These mutants resulted in loss of the tail-anchored client (SQS378-410) and partial loss of the N-terminal insertase-dependent polytopic client (B1AR), reflecting a failure to support insertase activity.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: Charge swap mutations along the rim of the gated cavity entrance (hEMC3E63K + D213K + E223K, hEMC3R59E + R62E + K216E) had no appreciable effect on the abundance of the polytopic transmembrane client (TMEM97) reporter.
source: These mutants had no appreciable effect on the abundance of the polytopic transmembrane client (TMEM97) reporter (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: Mutating a pair of adjacent asparagine residues to aspartates (hEMC3N114D+N117D) resulted in a dramatic decrease in SQS378-410 reporter levels and no significant decrease in the other two client reporter levels.
source: Mutating a pair of adjacent asparagine residues to equivalently sized but negatively charged aspartates (hEMC3N114D+N117D) resulted in a dramatic decrease in SQS378-410 reporter levels and no significant decrease in the other two client reporter levels (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: Western blot analysis for the hEMC3N114D+N117D mutant showed wild-type rescue levels of hEMC subunits and a decrease in endogenous SQS levels.
source: Western blot analysis for this mutant showed wild-type rescue levels of hEMC subunits and a decrease in endogenous SQS levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the western blot data presented.

claim: Mutating a conserved methionine to a leucine (hEMC3M151L) caused significant decrease in both SQS378-410 and B1AR abundance.
source: The importance of this hydrophobic seal is suggested by the strong effect of a structurally mild mutation of a conserved methionine to a leucine (hEMC3M151L), which caused significant decrease in both SQS378-410 and B1AR abundance (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: Mutation of a neighboring aromatic residue (hEMC3F148L) caused a decrease in all three client types without altering the levels of hEMC subunits.
source: Mutation of a neighboring aromatic residue (hEMC3F148L), contacting both a lipid and a hEMC4 C-terminal transmembrane helix, caused a decrease in all three client types without altering the levels of hEMC subunits (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: Proper EMC insertase function depends on the exact composition of the gated cavity and not simply on its hydrophobic nature.
source: Together these results indicate that proper EMC insertase function depends on the exact composition of the cavity and not simply on its hydrophobic nature.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is an inference based on the mutational data.

claim: While the core transmembrane helices of the gated cavity are superimposable in all four EMC structures, the adjacent gate helices appear in different relative orientations.
source: While the core transmembrane helices of the gated cavity are superimposable in all four of our EMC structures, the adjacent gate helices appear in different relative orientations.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The structural variability of the gate helices likely reflects dynamics of the gate.
source: The structural variability likely reflects dynamics of the gate (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Two major gate conformations were identified: a closed-gate conformation and an open-gate conformation.
source: Comparing detergent and nanodisc maps for both species identified two major gate conformations (Video 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 5A). One of the conformations, referred to as the closed-gate conformation, results in a more occluded membrane cavity. The other conformation, referred to as the open-gate conformation, would provide space for client accommodation.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The C-terminal transmembrane helix of EMC4 and ensuing lumenal segment are well resolved in all four EMC structures.
source: The C-terminal transmembrane helix of EMC4 and ensuing lumenal segment are well resolved in all four structures; however, other regions of EMC4, including the segment connecting the cytoplasmic domain to the transmembrane gate helices, were poorly resolved, perhaps owing to mobility.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Other regions of EMC4, including the segment connecting the cytoplasmic domain to the transmembrane gate helices, were poorly resolved, perhaps owing to mobility.
source: The C-terminal transmembrane helix of EMC4 and ensuing lumenal segment are well resolved in all four structures; however, other regions of EMC4, including the segment connecting the cytoplasmic domain to the transmembrane gate helices, were poorly resolved, perhaps owing to mobility.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The yEMC detergent map, yEMC nanodisc map, and hEMC detergent map all show the unassigned helices in the closed conformation, preventing client residence in the gated cavity.
source: The yEMC detergent map, yEMC nanodisc map, and hEMC detergent map all show the unassigned helices in the closed conformation, preventing client residence in the gated cavity.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The hEMC nanodisc map reveals an open-gate conformation with the unassigned helices shifted away from the transmembrane core to provide space for a client.
source: By contrast, the hEMC nanodisc map reveals an open-gate conformation with the unassigned helices shifted away from the transmembrane core to provide space for a client (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Mutating residues that together form a composite-binding surface for the cytoplasmic domain of hEMC4 (hEMC2E146A+E149A+Q150A, hEMC2E168A + D170A + K173A) resulted in a modest accumulation of the tail-anchored insertase client (SQS378-410).
source: As described above, mutating residues that together form a composite-binding surface for the cytoplasmic domain of hEMC4 (hEMC2E146A+E149A+Q150A, hEMC2E168A + D170A + K173A, Figure 3E–F), we observed a modest accumulation of the tail-anchored insertase client (SQS378-410).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: Mutating residues in the center of the gated cavity, close to one of the unassigned helices in the closed-gate conformation (hEMC3V118A + I122A) led to an increase of SQS378-410.
source: Likewise, mutating residues in the center of the gated cavity, close to one of the unassigned helices in the closed-gate conformation (hEMC3V118A + I122A) (Video 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) led to an increase of SQS378-410.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: Mutating a residue that contacts the lumenal anchor of hEMC4 (hEMC3F148L) caused a reduction of SQS378-410 levels.
source: This SQS378-410 accumulation effect stands in contrast to mutating a residue that contacts the lumenal anchor of hEMC4 (hEMC3F148L), which caused a reduction of SQS378-410 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: The surface of the lipid-filled cavity includes contributions from EMC1, EMC3, EMC5, and EMC6.
source: The surface of the lipid-filled cavity includes contributions from EMC1, EMC3, EMC5, and EMC6 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: In the EMC structures, the EMC2 N-terminus occludes cytoplasmic accessibility to the lipid-filled cavity.
source: In our structures, the EMC2 N-terminus occludes cytoplasmic accessibility to this cavity (Figure 4D, Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The lipid-filled cavity may be accessible from the membrane or the ER lumen.
source: However, this cavity may be accessible from the membrane or the ER lumen.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: The distance from the cytoplasmic EMC2 N-terminus to the lumenal side of the lipid-filled cavity is approximately 35 Å across, which is close to the average ER membrane thickness.
source: The respective distance from the cytoplasmic EMC2 N-terminus to the lumenal side of the lipid-filled cavity is approximately 35 Å across, which is close to the average ER membrane thickness (Mitra et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data and citation.

claim: The lipid-filled cavity features a uniformly hydrophobic surface.
source: The lipid-filled cavity features a uniformly hydrophobic surface (Figure 6C) and superimposes across our ensemble of EMC structures.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Several lipids were resolved in the cryo-EM maps lining the lipid-filled cavity wall and four POPC molecules were modeled in the hEMC nanodisc map.
source: As noted, we resolved several lipids in our cryo-EM maps lining the cavity wall and modeled four POPC (1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3 phosphatidylcholine) molecules in the hEMC nanodisc map (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the structural data presented.

claim: Most mutations of cavity-lining and lipid-proximal residues resulted in an increased abundance of the tail-anchored reporter (SQS378-410) and wild-type rescue levels for the other two reporters (B1AR, TMEM97).
source: Most of these mutations resulted in an increased abundance of the tail-anchored reporter (SQS378-410) and wild-type rescue levels for the other two reporters (B1AR, TMEM97).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by the mutational data presented.

claim: One lipid-proximal mutant (hEMC3R13E) showed decreased levels of all three client reporter types with varying severity without altering overall EMC levels.
